I am also having performance issues with the Android exports in base Godot 4.4 and I think I've identified the problem. Unfortunately I have not tested on other versions of Godot, but it wouldn't be hard to do yourself if you have a low end Android device.

**TL;DR**: The Android export template appears to be bugged in the Godot 4.4 stable installation, but works just fine in Godot-mono 4.4 stable, so maybe try running your app in Godot-mono to see if that fixes the issues you were seeing. The app size will be slightly larger, but not much else should change. You don't even need to use C#. Something about the templates is better on the mono installation. This is pretty undetectable on high end devices like Pixels and other flagships.

**How I came to this conclusion**
I have a very basic game I want to release soon and I'm targeting low end Android devices. The device I'm currently testing on has a Helio A22 chip and 60hz refresh rate. I've also tested on my personal phone which is a Pixel 6. The Pixel 6 was running my game fine. The Helio was not. I was getting 25-29fps. I tested out every optimization setting I could find for low end processors. Everything. I profiled a lot. Stripped out a ton of potentially non-optimal code. Nothing worked or even got me 1 frame back. Most things I tried made the frame rate worse. I started to accept that this was a "my phone" issue and that for some reason it was locked at 30hz even though the display was 60hz. 

But what bugged me is that I've run games like the one I want to make on this phone before with no lag whatsoever. So I tried making a much smaller test app that just had an FPS counter in the center of the screen. I was getting 29fps doing nothing. I added some basic physics simulation, it would drop a 2D ball when you tap the screen. While the balls were falling I'd get 27-28fps. So then I tried some blasphemy. I made the same basic physics sim in Unity. The Unity version was getting 30fps even without dipping even with 100s of balls dropped. (I learned later that I didn't set up my Unity project right, and by setting the target frame rate to 60 I was able to get 60fps). So I was solidifying my opinion that this is a "my phone" issue and my phone was stuck at 30fps fsr.

But it bugged me that Unity was getting 30fps even. Just a solid 30fps. And Godot was getting like 29fps. That seemed off to me. Godot has been plenty performant for my past projects. So I thought "what if it's a GDScript vs C# issue?" And I built the same test app in Godot-mono with a C# script instead. I ran it. AND GOT 60 FPS. Solid. No dips. I was so confused because the other test apps were <= 30fps (because I didn't know the right thing to do in Unity). I thought maybe this project was special or something. So in Godot-mono I switched to using GDScript and was getting 60fps still. I opened my original game up in Godot-mono and ran it with no changes (reset the settings changes from before) and I got a flawless 60fps.

I have since tried a few more times to get the base installation of Godot to work this well, including completely removing everything Godot related from my computer and reinstalling and building from scratch, and I can't get it to work. But Godot-mono works perfectly. The only issue is that it adds like 15MB to the APK size. For now I will keep developing my game in Godot-mono but just without using C# and hopefully this bug gets fixed for the non-mono installation soon.

I ran a quick experiment to try to understand where the performance loss is coming from exactly. For context, when merging the batching PR I had measured a slight GPU performance decrease on a few devices. We decided it was worthwhile to take on the slight decrease in GPU performance for a huge win in CPU performance. 

We may need to re-evaluate the decision going forward for a couple reasons:
1. The PR was made with Metal in mind since the overhead of additional draw calls was much higher with Metal on Apple devices than with Vulkan on other devices. With recent improvements to Metal, the draw call overhead may be much smaller. 
2. We can now take advantage of UMA
3. The performance impact on low end devices was more than we expected. 
4. More devices are GPU bottlenecked that we expected.

My theory is that the decrease in performance comes from a few things:
1. The shader emits less optimized code because everything depending on draw_data is dynamic instead of static across a draw call (i.e. the shader compiler can do fewer optimizations)
2. Mobile GPUs have to do expensive memory loads to read from SSBOs. Reading from a push constant or vertex buffer is much cheaper (this is why we use vertex buffers in the compatibility renderer) (I expect that this will have a bigger impact on mobile devices than the one above)

To test my theory. I replaced all instances of `instance_index` with `params.base_instance_index`. This should fully address item 1 above. It allows the compiler to make everything dependent on `draw_data` static across the draw call and do a lot of shader optimizations.

Using software-2's test project on my Intel integrated GPU (with 150 instances instead of 5) I saw a decrease in frame time from 26 mspf to 21.75 mspf. That's nearly a 20% increase from that simple change. Of course, that change only works for draw calls that aren't batched. 

Just for reference:
**4.3:** 13 mspf
**4.4:** 26 mspf
**my test:** 21.75 mspf

_edit: With 112481 that same test is down to 9.8 mspf :)_

@stuartcarnie I think this means we need to re-evaluate batching and consider the following options:
1. Remove batching in the RD renderers (might make sense if draw calls are cheap enough on metal now). If we do this, we need to add the multirect draw command though so that text and tilemaps can always be drawn in one draw call
2. Add a fast path for single item draw calls. If a batch only has a single item in it, we could fall back to a path that uses the push constant for the instance data instead. That would likely solve the issue for the MRP above, but may make our code a lot messier than it is now
3. Use vertex buffers for all the per-instance data. This would be a lot of work and makes the canvas shader a lot uglier (take a look at the compatibility renderer to see exactly how ugly), but it might allow us to have the best of both worlds. For context, the compatibility renderer renders software-2's test project at the same 13 mspf as 4.3 did. So that's a good indication that we can win back our previous performance
4. Attempt a totally different approach to batching. For a long time I have been stewing on the idea of breaking the data up into different caches. push constant / spec constant for per-batch data, vertex buffer or SSBO for per-instance data. This approach would need some testing and experimentation, but I think done well, could result in optimal performance

I would also measure power consumption (or battery drain over time) on devices that can reach their framerate target both with and without batching, as this is an important consideration for battery life. I expect batching to generally help with power consumption in most cases.

@clayjohn 

> * Remove batching in the RD renderers (might make sense if draw calls are cheap enough on metal now). If we do this, we need to add the multirect draw command though so that text and tilemaps can always be drawn in one draw call

I agree that without an alternative, we will almost certainly regress performance across a number of scenarios. From #92797:

| area | before | after |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| draw calls (for tile map) | > 573440 | 36 |
| FPS | ~10 | > 130 |

And this isn't just Metal, other users have reported performance issue with tile maps and text rendering, that are improved by batching. I would have to expect that even Vulkan benefits from batched draw calls rather than issuing thousands of individual API calls, particularly on mobile where the costs will be higher.

I wonder how 4.6 is with UMA buffers for the 2D rendering, since we're no longer performing multiple copies?
  
> * Add a fast path for single item draw calls. If a batch only has a single item in it, we could fall back to a path that uses the push constant for the instance data instead. That would likely solve the issue for the MRP above, but may make our code a lot messier than it is now

Presumably we'd have additional variants of the canvas shader to accommodate this?

> * Use vertex buffers for all the per-instance data. This would be a lot of work and makes the canvas shader a lot uglier (take a look at the compatibility renderer to see exactly how ugly), but it might allow us to have the best of both worlds. For context, the compatibility renderer renders software-2's test project at the same 13 mspf as 4.3 did. So that's a good indication that we can win back our previous performance

My understanding is that vertex buffers are faster because they are read-only and optimised for sequential access and handled by a specialised unit in the GPU?

This seems like it might be a worthy approach, as you noted we still get batching but also read the instance data via an optimised GPU path. We may even see further gains?

> * Attempt a totally different approach to batching. For a long time I have been stewing on the idea of breaking the data up into different caches. push constant / spec constant for per-batch data, vertex buffer or SSBO for per-instance data. This approach would need some testing and experimentation, but I think done well, could result in optimal performance

If you were to spec out your ideas that I could work from, we could look at that too. 

----

I wonder how much work it is to separate the CanvasRD renderer into its pieces, so that the base class provided the common API and shaders (canvas_occlusion.glsl, canvas_sdf.glsl), and we could then experiment with different 2D render implementations (variations of canvas.glsl). We could switch them at runtime to compare, making informed decisions much easier.

> I wonder how 4.6 is with UMA buffers for the 2D rendering, since we're no longer performing multiple copies?

I assume that there is some benefit across the board. It would be worth checking on a low end mobile device to confirm. But I suspect in the case in the MRP, it will have only a slight benefit since there is very little data transfer going on (50 passes with one draw call each)

> Presumably we'd have additional variants of the canvas shader to accommodate this?

That's right. Which is a problem currently since there is no ubershader system in place. This approach would necessarily double the up-front compile time for CanvasItems

> My understanding is that vertex buffers are faster because they are read-only and optimised for sequential access and handled by a specialised unit in the GPU?

That's part of it yes. The other part is that the shader compiler has more information about the source of information, its granularity, and how it can be used, so it can make more informed optimization decisions. 

> This seems like it might be a worthy approach, as you noted we still get batching but also read the instance data via an optimised GPU path. We may even see further gains?

Its possible. In the compatibility backend I saw improved GPU time on every device I tested when switching from using a UBO for batching to vertex buffers https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/70065. 

> I wonder how much work it is to separate the CanvasRD renderer into its pieces, so that the base class provided the common API and shaders (canvas_occlusion.glsl, canvas_sdf.glsl), and we could then experiment with different 2D render implementations (variations of canvas.glsl). We could switch them at runtime to compare, making informed decisions much easier.

Between using an SSBO and a vertex buffer I think this would be fairly easy since the data layout is the same. Almost everything can be kept the same. We would just need to create a shader variant and change the binding code and data upload code. 

For the big refactor approach, I think it would be more work than its worth, since that will also necessitate changing which conditions break batches. 

At this point, I am leaning in favour of just testing out the vertex buffer approach and seeing if we can easily win back performance. The main downside is you have to end up doing something like this in the code:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/c0c1c685621971c75c0f0f4aab85e8293c67a993/drivers/gles3/shaders/canvas.glsl#L42-L87

But using a vertex buffer has the benefit of being very flexible and being able to handle inefficient user-code really well. So it maintains reasonable performance in the worst case while having good performance in the best case.

Sounds good to me!

@software-2 Stuart's PR is now ready [#112481](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/112481) I have tested on a variety of devices and found that it helps a lot on most devices. 

I am not certain it will totally solve the issue on your Tab S9 FE+ since it has a low-end Mali GPU. The Mali GPU I tested didn't get much of a benefit from this PR since the bottleneck was elsewhere. However, I tested with 500 Viewports, so it is totally possible that the device has different bottlenecks than yours. 

I think further testing and investigation is needed to see why my Mali device isn't getting the same performance benefits as other devices. Also it hints that there may have been another change that impacted performance specifically for Mali devices. Although that would be surprising as for 4.4 we did a lot of rendering changes that benefited Mali devices (see this [blog post](https://developer.arm.com/community/arm-community-blogs/b/mobile-graphics-and-gaming-blog/posts/optimizing-3d-scenes-in-godot-on-arm-gpus))

At any rate, please test this PR if you can. If you can't, we will merge it soon and you can test with the next dev release!
